newsitem.title: MEXICO: Small bomb found, defused in central Mexico City.
newsitem.headline: Small bomb found, defused in central Mexico City.

text.p: Police defused a small homemade bomb planted at the central Mexico City Monument to the Revolution on Friday, two days before Independence Day celebrations, security sources said.

The find added to tension ahead of the Sunday night celebrations, at which tens of thousands of people were expected to throng to the city's central Zocalo square to hear President Ernesto Zedillo give the traditional "Cry of Independence."
Leftist rebels of the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) denied planning attacks on civilians during the celebrations.

The Mexican stock market was hit by news of the bomb find, coupled with speculation that EPR guerrillas may strike during the Independence celebrations and with the charging of a major newspaper editor with tax fraud.
"Specialists in explosive devices defused a homemade bomb this morning found at ... the Monument to the Revolution," a police source said.

"The device consisted of a one-litre plastic bottle containing a charge of gunpowder and nuts, screws and .45-calibre bullet cartridges as shrapnel," the source said. "It was not of great power but could have injured passers-by at the scene upon exploding."

Witnesses said the device, connected to a timer and placed in a shoebox at the foot of the monumental arch on the capital's main Reforma boulevard, was about one foot (35 cm) long and contained wiring and tubing bound together with tape.

Alongside it were found clippings from magazines, including pictures of starving African children, the late Latin American revolutionary Ernesto "Che" Guevara and the German imperial eagle, witnesses said. German Chancellor Helmut Kohl is due to visit Mexico next week.
Police sources said a warning about a second device had been received, but there were no other details.
Shortly before the close, the main stock market index was down 0.34 percent at 3,307.51, while the Dow Jones industrials scored a record high.

It was partly rocked by news that Juan Francisco Ealy Ortiz, editor of the major newspaper El Universal, had surrendered to police, denying charges of tax fraud and accusing the government of censorship.

"Although the (stock) market has been closely linked to developments in the U.S., what's affecting us is the political and social noise that just won't go away," Alejandro Mercado, an equity analyst at the Banorte brokerage, said.
The Monument to the Revolution, where the bomb was placed, sits on a square between the anti-narcotics agency and the Confederation of Mexican Workers trade union.
The incidents followed bomb threats in several cities in the last two weeks after the leftist Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) attacked the army and police in several southern states.

The EPR, in a statement carried by newspapers on Friday, denied threatening to attack civilians during Independence Day celebrations in the capital's main Zocalo square on Sept. 15. It said a supposed EPR communique carrying the threats, published by newspapers on Thursday, was false and part of an effort by the government to discredit the group.
The EPR surfaced in June in the southern state of Guerrero and carried out bloody attacks there and in Oaxaca state on the night of Aug. 28 in which at least 14 people died.
